patient.title: Docetaxel 75 mg/m² · previously treated NSCLC

agents.name: Docetaxel
agents.explanation: Docetaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules. Cells need these to separate their chromosomes during division; disrupting the process can stop cancer cells multiplying. Healthy dividing cells are also affected.
agents.watch: Take prescribed steroid premedication. Report fever, lasting numbness, swelling, sore nails or infusion symptoms.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and sepsis
Hair loss, mouth soreness and fatigue
Rare serious bowel inflammation or perforation
Rare serious lung or skin reactions; vision changes

support.title: Premedication
support.text: Take dexamethasone exactly as prescribed before and after docetaxel. Tell the unit about missed doses before infusion; any alternative needs the prescriber’s decision. Do not double a dose or add another steroid course yourself.

support.title: Nausea, bowel symptoms and pain
support.text: Use your individual anti-sickness and pain plan. Contact the team if symptoms are uncontrolled or you cannot drink. Antihistamines and other support medicines may cause drowsiness; arrange transport if advised.

support.title: Nerves and daily activities
support.text: Report tingling, numbness or weakness early, including effects on buttons, writing, walking or balance. Protect hands and feet and take care with hot surfaces if sensation changes.

support.title: Infection and blood counts
support.text: Each treatment needs its own blood and symptom review. A growth-factor injection may be prescribed after individual risk assessment; follow its separate instructions. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate contact on any day.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: A historical randomised trial found that docetaxel 75 mg/m² every three weeks prolonged survival compared with supportive care alone in selected people whose NSCLC had progressed after platinum chemotherapy. Modern previous treatment and available alternatives differ, so the trial cannot predict an individual outcome.
evidence.population: NCCP 00203a: locally advanced or metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer after failure of prior chemotherapy. This is docetaxel alone; a platinum or other partner needs its own regimen.
evidence.interpretation: Discuss possible benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own situation. The treatment aim is cancer control and symptom relief.
evidence.limitations: TAX317 was a historical randomised study after platinum chemotherapy; it predates current targeted therapy and immunotherapy. The 75 mg/m² cohort followed an initial 100 mg/m² cohort; preserve the dose-specific comparison and do not combine them as one 75 mg/m² estimate. NCCP limits this NSCLC course to six cycles. Trial results are population averages, not an individual survival prediction. TAX320 compared docetaxel with vinorelbine/ifosfamide; its overall survival comparison did not reach statistical significance. Do not imply all comparators showed the same result.

patient.title: Weekly paclitaxel · relapsed or refractory SCLC

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next weekly dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.
risks: Sensory or motor neuropathy, potentially persistent
Hair loss and nail / skin changes
Rare serious lung or cardiac effects
Rare serious bowel inflammation; vision changes

questions.q: What benefit is realistic for me and what other options are available?
questions.a: Treatment aims to control small-cell lung cancer after previous therapy and may help symptoms. The evidence is limited, so discuss likely benefit, burdens and alternatives with the team. A small uncontrolled study found some tumour responses to weekly paclitaxel in previously treated SCLC. The study used six weekly doses followed by two weeks without treatment, which differs from this NCCP schedule. It cannot establish a survival advantage over other treatment or supportive care.

questions.q: What are my confirmed infusion days, dose and planned review points?
questions.a: Paclitaxel 80 mg/m² is infused on Days 1, 8, 15 and 22 of a 28-day cycle. The consultant may instead prescribe Days 1, 8 and 15. Each planned weekly dose needs review. Continue while helping and tolerated; NCCP does not set a fixed cycle cap.

questions.q: Who arranges and reviews my blood tests and scans?
questions.a: FBC, kidney and liver profile at baseline and before each treatment; NCCP also explicitly lists Day 8 FBC. questions.a: Follow the written plan for your exact prescription. Report missed premedication before infusion; confirm prevention and rescue medicines with the pharmacist.

Keep the unit’s daytime and out-of-hours numbers on your treatment card.

day_groups.title: First visit of this cycle
day_groups.body: Review symptoms, blood results and premedication before the infusion. Tell the nurse straight away about itching, flushing, throat or chest tightness, back pain, dizziness or breathing change.
day_groups.action: Check transport if premedication makes you drowsy and confirm the next weekly visit.

day_groups.title: Between weekly doses
day_groups.body: Aches, fatigue, nausea or bowel symptoms may occur. Tingling may be mild at first but matters before the next dose. Record what symptoms stop you doing.
day_groups.action: Contact the team for new or worsening numbness, balance trouble, marked weakness or uncontrolled symptoms. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate contact.

day_groups.title: Second weekly review
day_groups.body: This dose requires its own symptom and blood-test review. Describe the worst symptoms since the previous visit, not only how you feel today.
day_groups.action: Report sensory changes before the infusion and confirm your premedication instructions.

day_groups.title: Keep tracking function
day_groups.body: Repeated treatment can increase nerve symptoms and fatigue. Check practical tasks such as buttons, writing and walking. Use the symptom passport to show changes.
day_groups.action: Seek early advice rather than waiting until numbness is severe.

day_groups.title: Third weekly review
day_groups.body: The team decides whether treatment can proceed using the current assessment.
day_groups.action: Confirm whether Day 22 is planned for you; do not infer this from a different person’s calendar.

day_groups.title: After the third visit
day_groups.body: Symptoms may settle or continue. An interval between appointments does not rule out infection or a treatment complication.
day_groups.action: Use the urgent contact plan if unwell and bring your record to the next review.

day_groups.title: Day 22: follow the prescribed schedule
day_groups.body: A fourth dose is part of the four-visit plan. In the consultant-selected three-visit plan there is no Day 22 infusion. The calendar here is educational.
day_groups.action: Use your confirmed appointment and prescription; call if the schedule is unclear.

day_groups.title: Complete the cycle record
day_groups.body: Record symptoms and functional changes, including those that improve before the next appointment. Treatment continuation depends on benefit, toxicity and your priorities.
day_groups.action: Check the next cycle date and review plan. Do not treat a gap in visits as a guarantee of recovery.

support.title: Premedication
support.text: Premedication reduces infusion-reaction risk. The first-dose and later-dose plans may differ under the NCCP weekly pathway. The team must reconcile your exact product and reaction history; do not omit premedication yourself.

support.title: Nausea, bowel symptoms and pain
support.text: Use your individual anti-sickness and pain plan. Contact the team if symptoms are uncontrolled or you cannot drink. Antihistamines and other support medicines may cause drowsiness; arrange transport if advised.

support.title: Nerves and daily activities
support.text: Report tingling, numbness or weakness early, including effects on buttons, writing, walking or balance. Protect hands and feet and take care with hot surfaces if sensation changes.

support.title: Infection and blood counts
support.text: Each treatment needs its own blood and symptom review. A growth-factor injection may be prescribed after individual risk assessment; follow its separate instructions. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate contact on any day.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: A small uncontrolled study found some tumour responses to weekly paclitaxel in previously treated SCLC. The study used six weekly doses followed by two weeks without treatment, which differs from this NCCP schedule. It cannot establish a survival advantage over other treatment or supportive care.
evidence.population: NCCP 00226d: small-cell lung cancer that has returned or has not responded to previous treatment. This use is outside the Irish licence and requires the hospital off-label approval and consent process. This guide is for conventional paclitaxel alone.
evidence.interpretation: Discuss possible benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own situation. The treatment aim is cancer control and symptom relief.
evidence.limitations: Yamamoto 2006 enrolled 22 patients, with 21 eligible; it was a small single-arm phase II study without a control group. The trial schedule was 80 mg/m² weekly for six weeks of an eight-week cycle, not the NCCP Day 1/8/15/22 28-day schedule or its three-of-four-week alternative. Five partial responses were observed: three of 11 sensitive and two of 10 refractory cases. These counts are not a comparative efficacy estimate. The study cannot establish a survival benefit, modern treatment ranking or the expected response probability for the current NCCP schedule. NCCP explicitly flags 00226d as off-label; publication and NCCP listing do not create an Irish product licence.

clinical.component_rationale: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.

support_summary: NCCP first-dose suggested premedication: dexamethasone 8 mg IV, chlorphenamine 10 mg IV and famotidine 20 mg IV 30 minutes before infusion.

From Day 8, NCCP permits omission of routine dexamethasone; previous reaction or higher risk requires consultant-directed adjustment. Famotidine omission is also a consultant/local-policy decision with close observation.
The actual conventional product SmPC uses a different generic premedication schedule. Reconcile the exact product and local protocol; no automatic patient-led omission or switch to nab-paclitaxel.
Consider analgesia for muscle/joint aches; review neuropathy before every dose and growth-factor support when indicated.
Low emetic risk: prevention and rescue medicines remain separate from reaction premedication. Confirm individual suitability, interactions and duration; this reference is not a prescription.
